overview: This period's genuinely new activity is less about another model family and more about research hardening around deployment constraints. The adaptive memory and continual-adaptation work is accelerating fastest: the cluster around KV-cache compression, hybrid attention transfer, and replay-free continual pretraining is now explicitly attacking the HBM, context-length, and forgetting ceilings that production LLM stacks still treat as fixed. Agent research remains active but the center of gravity is shifting from capability demos to executable evaluation and system-level security, especially around indirect prompt injection and hidden process failures. In applied modeling, both neural physics surrogates and structured probabilistic forecasting are converging on physics- or causality-aware inductive bias rather than generic black-box scaling. The previously prominent sparse high-resolution visual routing direction appears to be stalling relative to these newer systems-constrained clusters, while dynamic LLM evaluation remains important but is not accelerating at the same rate.

macro_patterns.name: Memory-locality pressure in LLM adaptation
macro_patterns.summary: The adaptive inference-time reasoning and memory cluster and the dynamic LLM evaluation protocols cluster are both converging on a systems reality that benchmark gains increasingly come from how models manage context, cache state, and adaptation rather than from larger dense backbones. Papers on adaptive KV-cache quantization, latent/low-rank attention, and hybrid transformer conversion all point at the same non-research constraint: HBM bandwidth and device memory now dominate long-context serving economics, while most production stacks still assume dense full-attention decoding with coarse cache controls.
macro_patterns.so_what: Serving advantage shifts from raw model size to memory-bandwidth efficiency and state-management policy; long-context inference becomes a systems margin business before it becomes a model-quality business.

macro_patterns.name: Executable trust layers for agents
macro_patterns.summary: The executable agent evaluation cluster and the agent security/jailbreak cluster are converging on the same framing: model-level safety tests miss the failures that matter once an agent can act through tools, repos, browsers, and APIs. Research is moving toward execution-grounded evaluation, action-graph observability, and stateful attack/defense models, all because the real constraint is operational risk and auditability rather than raw benchmark accuracy.
macro_patterns.so_what: Buyer trust shifts from 'which model scored highest' to 'which system can expose, replay, and constrain every agent action under attack'; opaque agent wrappers get commoditized.

macro_patterns.name: Physics-aware surrogates under data scarcity
macro_patterns.summary: The neural operator/physics-surrogate cluster and the probabilistic time-series forecasting cluster both move away from generic sequence learners toward architectures that bake in transport, causality, conservation, or decomposition structure. The shared non-research constraint is data and compute cost: high-fidelity simulation, industrial telemetry, and weather data are expensive enough that brute-force scaling of generic transformers is economically inferior to structured models.
macro_patterns.so_what: In scientific and industrial prediction, the moat moves from foundation-model scale to sample efficiency under physical constraints; generic forecasters lose pricing power where every training trajectory is expensive.

clusters.label: KV-cache and continual adaptation
clusters.one_line: This cluster combines long-context inference efficiency with architectural approaches to continual LLM adaptation that avoid catastrophic forgetting.
clusters.existing_landscape: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, LMDeploy, and Fireworks already optimize LLM serving, including paged KV caches, continuous batching, and quantization-aware deployment. For adaptation, LoRA and QLoRA are standard across Hugging Face PEFT, Axolotl, Unsloth, Together, and Databricks workflows, while model vendors like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google mostly expose fine-tuning or prompt/context-level adaptation rather than persistent architectural memory. These stacks overlap on one assumption: the base transformer remains architecturally fixed, and adaptation is either parameter-efficient fine-tuning or external retrieval, not dynamic memory specialization inside the model.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The research is exposing two missing capabilities that the shipping landscape largely does not offer. First, papers like LightTransfer, Multi-Head Low-Rank Attention, and adaptive KV-cache quantization show that a pretrained transformer can be converted or routed into materially more memory-local long-context variants without retraining from scratch, but mainstream serving stacks still optimize around the original dense architecture instead of exposing architecture-level cache topology changes. Second, Sparse Memory Finetuning, TFGN, and attribution-guided continual learning point toward replay-free or semantically localized updates that preserve prior capabilities, whereas production fine-tuning from OpenAI, Anthropic-integrators, and Hugging Face-centric pipelines still assume either offline retraining, LoRA overlays, or retrieval as the answer to new knowledge. The gap is not 'better tuning'; it is that industry products still treat inference state and learned memory as separate layers even as research converges on hybrid internal-memory mechanisms.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is GROWING and large, with a 46.5% week-over-week jump from an already important adaptive inference line. LightTransfer and the recent adaptive KV-cache quantization paper sharpen the hardware-side gap, while TFGN sharpens the continual-learning side by claiming task-free, replay-free continual pretraining at LLM scale.
clusters.risks: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or model providers could absorb much of the serving-side gap as new cache formats or attention kernels. The continual-adaptation side is riskier because many claims fail when moved from benchmark tasks to messy enterprise updates, and retrieval systems remain the incumbent workaround.

clusters.label: Agent-system attack observability
clusters.one_line: This cluster studies jailbreaks, indirect prompt injection, and runtime detection at the agent-system level rather than at the standalone model level.
clusters.existing_landscape: Lakera, Protect AI, HiddenLayer, Robust Intelligence, Microsoft Prompt Shields, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, and Lakera Guard all offer pieces of LLM security such as prompt-injection filtering, red teaming, or policy guardrails. LangSmith, Weights & Biases Weave, Arize Phoenix, Helicone, and OpenTelemetry-style tracing provide observability for LLM applications, while OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google provide model-side safety filters. The overlap is substantial, but most products still assume the main unit of defense is a prompt/response exchange or a model endpoint, with limited visibility into hidden tool actions, cross-step state, or decomposed multi-turn attacks.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research is converging on the fact that the meaningful attack surface is the execution graph of the compound AI system, not the model output alone. Papers on indirect prompt injection, AgentSeer-style action graphs, TwinGate's stateful defense, and Layerwise Convergence Fingerprinting all point to failures that remain invisible if a platform only scores final responses or blocks known bad prompts. None of the named security vendors has established a standard, widely deployed control plane for action-level provenance, replayable attack paths, and stateful detection across anonymized, interleaved sessions; their offerings are still mostly wrappers around model I/O or policy classification. The gap is especially sharp because the recent position paper argues swarm attacks and software vulnerability discovery are already achievable on commodity hardware, collapsing the cost barrier for attackers.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is NEW and large, and several recent papers sharpen the same point from different angles: the public competition paper on indirect prompt injection highlights concealment, and TwinGate raises the bar by treating decompositional jailbreaks under anonymous traffic as the realistic threat model.
clusters.risks: Security incumbents like Microsoft, NVIDIA, Lakera, or Protect AI can extend existing guardrail and tracing products into richer action-graph observability. Some of the research threat models may also be ahead of current enterprise deployment reality outside high-autonomy agents.

clusters.label: Physics-constrained neural surrogates
clusters.one_line: This cluster centers on neural architectures and training schemes that make scientific simulators, operator learners, and black-box physical components more data- and compute-efficient.
clusters.existing_landscape: NVIDIA Modulus, PhysicsNeMo, Ansys, Siemens, COMSOL-adjacent workflows, and Altair all address parts of physics-informed ML or simulation acceleration, while open-source projects like DeepXDE, PhiFlow, and NeuralOperator cover research-to-engineering pipelines. For hardware-aware non-differentiable learning, there are real efforts in photonic and neuromorphic computing, but there is no single dominant commercial stack exposing standardized training for black-box physical layers. Across this landscape, most shipped systems still assume either differentiable surrogates trained with conventional backpropagation or expensive classical solvers augmented by ML at the margins.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The recent papers point to a more radical shift than 'physics-informed regularization.' Mesh-based surrogates with spatial-temporal awareness, DGNet's discrete Green-function framing, and causally or structurally sparse operator learners all encode numerical method structure directly, while PolyStep and related zero-order work make non-differentiable or physical components trainable with forward-only updates. Industry platforms have not normalized this combination: simulation vendors still sell accuracy against classical solvers, and ML platforms mostly treat black-box layers, sparse structural plasticity, or hardware-in-the-loop components as bespoke research integrations. The gap is the absence of a standard deployment substrate for surrogates whose core advantage is not just speed, but compatibility with stiff dynamics, sparse operators, and non-backprop trainability under real hardware constraints.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is NEW and sizeable, and the representative papers attack the same bottleneck from complementary sides: data-efficient PDE learning, numerically faithful surrogate structure, and training through non-differentiable components. That combination makes the direction look more like convergence than isolated novelty.
clusters.risks: NVIDIA and major simulation vendors have enough adjacent distribution to incorporate much of this as product features, especially on the PDE-surrogate side. Also, many surrogate papers overfit benchmark families and underdeliver on industrial geometry, boundary-condition variation, or certification requirements.

clusters.label: Causality- and physics-aware forecasting
clusters.one_line: This cluster develops forecasting models that explicitly represent transport, periodic structure, causal dependencies, and uncertainty rather than treating time series as generic token sequences.
clusters.existing_landscape: Nixtla, Datadog, IBM, Salesforce, AWS Forecast's legacy ecosystem, Azure time-series tooling, and industrial vendors like Seeq and AVEVA cover forecasting, anomaly detection, and operations monitoring. Weather-focused groups such as ECMWF, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and Huawei have shipped or published ML weather systems, while open-source libraries like GluonTS, NeuralForecast, darts, and PyTorch Forecasting support mainstream deep forecasting workflows. Most of these offerings still assume either generic sequence models or black-box foundation forecasters, with causality and physical structure handled post hoc if at all.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The representative papers converge on a capability the market does not expose cleanly: forecasting systems that treat causal structure, advection, and regime-dependent decomposition as first-class model components and evaluation targets. PARADIS hard-codes semi-Lagrangian transport for weather, the causally guided transformer ties anomaly detection to root-cause structure, and noise-titration benchmarking attacks the industry's weak habit of validating on passive historical splits. Existing commercial stacks can forecast and alert, but they rarely distinguish correlation-fitting from intervention-relevant predictive structure, which matters when operators need trustworthy anomaly localization or stable extrapolation under shift. The gap is strongest where errors are expensive and the binding constraint is scarce fault data or high cost of distribution shift, not leaderboard RMSE.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is NEW, and several May papers reinforce the same structured-model direction rather than a one-off architecture trend. The weather and industrial examples make the constraint legible: global attention and generic token mixers are too compute-hungry or too weakly grounded for many real forecasting settings.
clusters.risks: Much of this can be folded into incumbent forecasting platforms as model options, especially by weather and industrial analytics vendors with domain distribution. Also, causal claims in time-series work are often brittle when intervention assumptions are violated.

clusters.label: Executable agent evaluation
clusters.one_line: This cluster focuses on evaluating software and research agents through executable environments, process tracing, and collaboration diagnostics rather than static benchmarks.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI Codex CLI, Anthropic Claude Code, Cognition Devin, OpenHands, SWE-agent, LangSmith, Braintrust, Weights & Biases Weave, HumanEval-style benchmarks, and SWE-bench already cover slices of agent development and evaluation. E2B and Modal provide execution sandboxes, while software engineering orgs increasingly run internal harnesses for repository tasks. The common assumption is that outcome metrics on benchmark tasks plus traces are enough to compare agents, even though execution setups, hidden prompts, and environmental details vary wildly across reports.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The recent work argues that agent evaluation needs to be reproducible, executable, and process-aware at the environment level, not just benchmark-score based. AgentCollabBench shows that good individual agents can still fail systematically in collaboration, AutoControl Arena decouples deterministic executable state from generative dynamics for risk evaluation, and the reproducibility review highlights how little of today's agent evaluation can actually be rerun faithfully. Despite many developer tools, no widely adopted evaluation standard spans executable state, tool permissions, collaboration protocols, and hidden-process failure modes across software agents. This leaves buyers comparing glossy benchmark numbers produced under incompatible harness assumptions.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is only STABLE, but the gap has sharpened because the representative papers are moving beyond 'agents on SWE-bench' to executable risk environments and collaboration failure diagnosis. As agent products ship into real SDLC workflows, the evaluation mismatch matters more commercially than another small benchmark gain.
clusters.risks: LangSmith, Braintrust, OpenAI, Anthropic, or benchmark maintainers can close much of this by adding richer environment capture and standardized replay. The cluster is also crowded with surveys and meta-evaluation papers, so not all activity implies a durable gap.

clusters.label: Variance-aware RLVR optimization
clusters.one_line: This cluster improves reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning models by targeting rollout allocation, exploration, off-policy reuse, and noisy reward handling.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and xAI all use some form of post-training with RL or RL-like optimization for reasoning models, while open-source stacks such as TRL, OpenRLHF, verl, Axolotl, and various GRPO implementations support practitioners. Inference providers and model API vendors generally expose the resulting models, not the training control systems behind them. The shared assumption is that enough compute can wash out poor sample efficiency, high gradient variance, and reward noise.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The cluster's papers increasingly treat RLVR as a compute-allocation problem under expensive rollouts, not just an algorithmic afterthought. DynaMO, DYPO, ReVal, and ODRPO all attack wasted trajectories, variance collapse, or stochastic auto-raters, yet there is little evidence that commercial post-training stacks expose fine-grained rollout budgeting, off-policy reuse, or reward-noise-aware controls as first-class primitives. The gap matters because reasoning-model training is becoming constrained by verification cost and long-horizon rollout expense, not merely by parameter count. Industry has built model endpoints and generic RL tooling; research is converging on training-efficiency levers for a workload whose unit economics are getting worse.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is not NEW but remains large with solid growth, and recent papers sharpen the constraint from multiple sides: compute allocation, exploration under sparse rewards, and robustness to stochastic judges. That breadth suggests a maturing bottleneck rather than isolated tuning tricks.
clusters.risks: Frontier labs likely already implement parts of these ideas internally, which limits how non-obvious the gap is from the outside. Open-source RLHF/RLVR frameworks can also adopt these methods quickly once they stabilize.
